arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: the side that brought the case Timothy Jones stated his property suffers damage from water leaking out of the Madera Canal.
Jones described the canal as an irrigation facility that passes water to Madera County farmers.
Government advocate Frederick explained that multiple-purpose projects operate like the Friant Division.
Frederick noted the Friant Dam collects water to avert flooding along the San Joaquin River. He added that the project gradually releases water to serve both flood control and irrigation needs.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The dispute centers on whether the government must compensate private landowners for water damage. The water originates from a canal serving both flood control and irrigation.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case seeks monetary compensation for property damage caused by leaking canal water.
The government seeks to avoid paying compensation for water released from a dual-purpose project.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues the government must pay because the canal is an irrigation facility causing direct damage.
The government argues the project serves multiple purposes, including flood control, which changes liability.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines when the government must pay for water damage from public infrastructure. It sets the standard for liability involving dual-purpose water projects. The outcome determines financial responsibility for farmers affected by canal leaks.
